paper_title: CurvDelta: Low-Curvature Delta Modeling For Surgical Learning and Unlearning

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: A central challenge in adapting large language models (LLMs) is capability preservation: an adaptation can achieve its target while degrading general capabilities. We introduce CurvDelta, a scalable framework that incorporates the preservation constraint into the parameterization of the model update. By analyzing the local geometry of the preservation constraint around the pre-adaptation model, CurvDelta constructs a low-curvature space in which parameter updates leave the preservation loss nearly invariant. We make its construction practical for LLMs through Kronecker-factored approximate curvature (K-FAC) and a factorized projection. We also introduce CurvLoRA, a low-rank variant within the same preservation geometry, designed for more efficient adaptation. Both methods apply to preservation-constrained adaptation tasks such as capability learning and selective unlearning. We evaluate our methods on mathematical reasoning, code generation, and knowledge unlearning. For mathematical reasoning and code generation, our approaches achieve competitive downstream performance while better preserving general capabilities, offering a favorable acquisition--retention trade-off relative to the baselines. For knowledge unlearning, our main results on TOFU and MUSE show a better balance between targeted forgetting and knowledge retention than the baselines, with retention performance close to the from-scratch retraining reference.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Large language models (LLMs) need to evolve after pretraining. New tasks and domains call for additional capabilities, while privacy, safety, and data-governance requirements can necessitate selective unlearning. Retraining from scratch for every adaptation query is costly, motivating finetuning and parameter-efficient methods for capability learning and selective unlearning (Hu et al., 2022; Cao & Yang, 2015; Maini et al., 2024; Shi et al., 2025). Although learning and unlearning change behavior in different ways, both require the update to be selective: progress on the target objective should preserve unrelated knowledge and capabilities. To preserve existing capabilities while allowing the changes needed for adaptation, prior work has introduced different approaches to limiting unwanted changes. Replay and regularization incorporate preservation into the training objective (Rolnick et al., 2019; Kirkpatrick et al., 2017). Another line of work constrains the space in which adaptation may move, either by projecting task gradients (Chaudhry et al., 2019; Ikram et al., 2026) or by heuristically restricting adaptation to orthogonal or null subspaces of parameters or representations (Fang et al., 2025; Xiong & Xie, 2026; Ju et al., 2026; Liang & Li, 2024; Luo et al., 2026). Despite improvements, these methods either do not guarantee that the parameter update satisfies the intended constraint or impose strong constraints in parameter or representation space that are only indirectly tied to capability preservation. These limitations can lead to an unfavorable adaptationpreservation trade-off. In this paper, we adopt first-principles formulation of preservation-constrained adaptation. We seek model delta that minimizes the task loss subject to bound on the preservation loss, which measures changes in the models behavior on designated preservation set. We therefore ask: Equal contribution. 1Project page: https://xiaozi-max.github.io/CurvDelta/ 1 Preprint. Figure 1: Overview of CurvDelta. (a) Unconstrained optimization reaches low task loss but high preservation loss. (b) CurvDelta constructs low-curvature delta space. The applied delta remains in this space throughout optimization, reaching different solution with comparable task loss. (c) The base weights and projections remain frozen. The trainable delta is dense matrix in CurvDelta or LoRA in CurvLoRA. (d) Performance comparison. The dashed line marks the base models retention average. Our methods achieve the best trade-off between task performance and capability retention. (Q) How can we directly incorporate the preservation constraint into the model delta parameterization while retaining the flexibility needed for adaptation? To address this question, we introduce CurvDelta, framework for low-curvature delta modeling for surgical learning and unlearning (Figure 1). CurvDelta learns dense delta within fixed lowcurvature space. We also introduce CurvLoRA, low-rank variant that uses the same preservation geometry for more efficient adaptation. The method is built around the following three core ideas. 1. Preservation through task-independent delta parameterization. CurvDelta derives lowcurvature delta space from the local geometry of the preservation constraint around the pre-adaptation model. It constrains trainable delta into this fixed space before applying it, keeping the realized update constrained throughout optimization. Because the space depends only on the base model and preservation set, the same preservation geometry can be reused across task sets, task objectives, and delta parameterizations. 2. Scalable delta space construction for dense and low-rank adaptation. To make low-curvature delta space construction tractable at LLM scale, CurvDelta approximates preservation curvature with block-diagonal Kronecker-factored approximate curvature (K-FAC) (Martens & Grosse, 2015). It further applies factorwise spectral truncation to obtain separable two-sided projection that can be stored and applied efficiently using compact eigenvector bases. The same construction supports both dense adaptation in CurvDelta and low-rank adaptation in CurvLoRA. 3. An explicit preservation guarantee from curvature and displacement. We show that preservation is jointly controlled by the curvature of the retained delta space and the magnitude of the realized 2 Preprint. update. Specifically, we derive an upper bound on the local preservation loss in which curvature determines the cost per unit displacement, while the delta norm determines the total displacement. Under the local quadratic and block-diagonal K-FAC models, this bound provides sufficient condition for both CurvDelta and CurvLoRA to satisfy the preservation constraint. Experimental results. We evaluate our framework on capability learning and selective unlearning. For capability learning, we study mathematical reasoning and code generation together with retention of general knowledge. Our approach achieves competitive downstream performance while reducing degradation in general capabilities, yielding favorable acquisitionretention trade-off relative to the evaluated baselines. For selective unlearning, our main results on TOFU and MUSE show better balance between targeted forgetting and knowledge retention than the evaluated baselines. On TOFU, our approach suppresses targeted knowledge while maintaining utility comparable to the retraining reference. On MUSE, it substantially reduces targeted memorization while retaining most of the retrained models performance.

sections.title: 2 PROBLEM FORMULATION: PRESERVATION-CONSTRAINED ADAPTATION
sections.content: Let θ0 be the initial parameter vector of language model. We write θ = θ0 + θ for the adapted parameters, with θ the update, and pθ for the distribution induced by θ. Preservation-constrained adaptation seeks an update θ that achieves specified behavior change while leaving unrelated behaviors intact. Each adaptation can be described by task set Dtask, which encodes the desired behavior, and preservation set Dpres, which marks behavior that should remain unchanged. For capability learning, Dtask contains data from new task; for selective unlearning, it contains examples of the behavior to be removed. Dpres may comprise pretraining data or representative proxy dataset. Let Ltask(θ) denote the task loss on Dtask. We define the preservation loss as Lpres(θ) = ExDpres [d(zθ(x), zθ0(x))], where zθ(x) denotes the model output vector and measures its deviation from the original output. We then formulate preservation-constrained adaptation as the following constrained optimization problem: min θ Ltask(θ) s.t. Lpres(θ) ε, (1) where ε > 0 specifies the tolerated preservation drift. This formulation covers both acquiring new capability and removing targeted behavior, with only the choice of Ltask distinguishing the two. standard way to optimize this problem is to minimize the Lagrangian Ltask(θ) + λ Lpres(θ), with λ 0 controlling the taskpreservation trade-off. This relaxation has two limitations. First, λ does not translate into the tolerance ε of Eq. (1): the drift is known only after training. Second, the Lagrangian is itself multi-task objective, and gradient conflict makes the two objectives difficult to satisfy jointly (Yu et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2021; Chen et al., 2020), especially in unlearning (Xiao et al., 2026a).

sections.title: 4 EXPERIMENTS
sections.content: We summarize the setup and main results here, and provide the experimental details in Appendix E.

sections.title: 4.1.1 EXPERIMENTAL SETUP
sections.content: Tasks, datasets, and evaluation. We study capability acquisition in mathematical reasoning and code generation. For mathematical reasoning, we fine-tune on 100K examples sampled from MetaMathQA (Yu et al., 2024) and evaluate on GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021) and MATH (Hendrycks et al., 2021b). For code generation, we fine-tune on 104K examples sampled from CodeFeedback (Zheng et al., 2024) and evaluate on HumanEval (Chen et al., 2021) and MBPP (Austin et al., 2021). To measure knowledge retention, we evaluate on TriviaQA (Joshi et al., 2017), NQ-Open (Kwiatkowski et al., 2019), and MMLU (Hendrycks et al., 2021a). For the preservation set Dpres, we use 256 examples sampled from the FineFineWeb corpus (M-A-P et al., 2024). Models. We evaluate both tasks using the pretrained base checkpoints of Gemma-3-1B (Gemma Team et al., 2025) and Llama-2-7B (Touvron et al., 2023). For PEFT methods and CurvLoRA, we set the rank to 128 for Gemma-3-1B and 32 for Llama-2-7B, holding it fixed across tasks. Baselines. We include standard fine-tuning (FT) as an unconstrained adaptation reference and experience replay (Replay) (Rolnick et al., 2019) as data-based baseline. Replay mixes task examples with examples sampled from Dpres during fine-tuning. We additionally include CrispEdit (Ikram et al., 2026) as curvature-based gradient-projection baseline and OPLoRA (Xiong & Xie, 2026) as an orthogonal delta-projection baseline. We further compare against LoRA (Hu et al., 2022), PiSSA (Meng et al., 2024), MiLoRA (Wang et al., 2025a), and the knowledge-preserved version of CorDA (Yang et al., 2024).

sections.title: 4.2.1 EXPERIMENTAL SETUP
sections.content: Benchmarks and models. We conduct experiments on two widely-used LLM unlearning benchmarks: TOFU (Maini et al., 2024) and MUSE (Shi et al., 2025). TOFU provides controlled unlearning setting based on synthetic author-profile QA pairs, whereas MUSE evaluates verbatim and knowledge memorization on real-world text corpora. For TOFU, we evaluate the Forget 5% and Forget 10% settings on three instruction-tuned backbones spanning 3B8B scales: Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct (Grattafiori et al., 2024), Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 (Yang et al., 2025), and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (Grattafiori et al., 2024). We omit the Forget 1% setting because it is too weak to distinguish methods. For MUSE, we use the benchmarks Llama-2-7B target model on the Books corpus. Further details are provided in Appendix E.2. Baselines and objectives. We compare CurvLoRA and CurvDelta against five baselines: full fine-tuning (FT), CrispEdit (Ikram et al., 2026), LoRA (Hu et al., 2022), VILA (Kim et al., 2025), and OPLoRA (Xiong & Xie, 2026). FT, LoRA, VILA, and OPLoRA represent full-parameter, standard parameter-efficient, unlearning-specific parameterizations, and orthogonal delta-projection adaptation, respectively, while CrispEdit is curvature-based gradient-projection method. Each method is evaluated with three unlearning objectives: Gradient Difference (GradDiff) (Liu et al., 2022; Maini et al., 2024), Negative Preference Optimization (NPO) (Zhang et al., 2024), and SimNPO (Fan et al., 2025). Appendices and E.2 provide the objective definitions and optimization settings, respectively. Evaluation. For TOFU, we report three core metrics: Forget Quality (FQ), QA probability (FP), and model utility (MU). FQ is based on KS-test p-value that checks whether the unlearned model and model retrained from scratch without the forget data behave similarly on the forget examples. We report the base-10 logarithm of this p-value in the TOFU tables and denote the retrained model Retrain. For MUSE, we report forget verbatim memorization (VerbMem), forget knowledge memorization (KnowMem), and retain knowledge memorization (Retain KnowMem), all measured by ROUGE.

sections.title: 4.3 ABLATION STUDIES
sections.content: We study four design choices on TOFU Forget 10% (with Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct and SimNPO), chosen as controlled setting with an exact Retrain reference. Specifically, we examine the projection basis, the spectral-energy threshold γ, and the preservation-data ratio (Figure 2), as well as delta parameterization versus gradient projection (Figure 3). Projection basis. To isolate the effect of direction selection, we compare our low-curvature delta space with two dimension-matched variants constructed from high-curvature and random directions. As shown in Figure 2 (a), across learning rates, updates in the low-curvature space strengthen forgetting while maintaining model utility, whereas both variants lose utility at the largest learning rate while still producing weaker forgetting. These comparisons show that constructing the delta space from preservation curvature improves the forgettingutility trade-off beyond its dimension. Spectral-energy threshold. The threshold γ jointly controls the maximum retained curvature and the dimension of the available update space. As shown in Figure 2 (b), all thresholds strengthen forgetting relative to LoRA with comparable model utility; larger γ generally further reduces QA probability while utility remains stable. Preservation-data ratio. We estimate curvature from subsets of the retain set, with sizes from 0.25 to 4 that of the forget set. As shown in Figure 2 (c), the performance of CurvLoRA is robust to the amount of preservation data used for curvature estimation, indicating that our method does not require large preservation set to estimate an effective low-curvature space. Delta parameterization vs. gradient projection. To separate delta parameterization from subspace selection, we compare CurvDelta with gradient-projection variant (CurvDeltaGrad) that projects task gradients with the same fixed (P out , in ) before each Adam step rather than parameterizing Wl = out δlP in . As shown in Figure 3, CurvDelta achieves higher Forget Quality and model utility across learning rates at comparable QA probability (detailed values in Appendix Table 12), confirming the benefit of keeping the applied update within the low-curvature space under adaptive optimization. 9 Figure 3: Delta parameterization vs. gradient projection. (b) Empirical retain-set KL across methods. (c) Total wall-clock runtime and peak GPU memory.

sections.title: 5.1 PRESERVATION LOSS AND THEORETICAL BOUND
sections.content: Continuing with the same TOFU setting, Figure 4 (a) compares the empirical retain-set KL of CurvLoRA with the K-FAC quadratic approximation and the spectral bound in Eq. (8) across learning rates and thresholds γ (detailed values in Appendix Table 13). The K-FAC quadratic approximation remains below the spectral bound in every configuration. Although the local quadratic model around θ0 operates on smaller numerical scale than the full-training retain-set KL, all three quantities share the same monotonic trends: larger γ removes more leading curvature directions and lowers all three values at each learning rate, whereas larger learning rates increase them. Across adaptation methods in Figure 4 (b), CurvDelta yields substantially lower retain-set KL than full fine-tuning and CrispEdit, and CurvLoRA attains the lowest retain-set KL among the low-rank methods.

sections.title: 5.2 COMPUTATIONAL EFFICIENCY
sections.content: Figure 4 (c) compares end-to-end wall-clock runtime (including curvature estimation) and peak GPU memory across methods (detailed values in Appendix Table 14). Caching only the thin leading factor eigenbases rather than the full factor eigenbases and product mask required by CrispEdit enables CurvDelta to substantially cut total runtime with lower peak memory. Projecting low-rank factors directly in CurvLoRA further reduces peak memory relative to the dense variant while matching the runtime of OPLoRA. Moreover, because the cached eigenbases depend only on the base model, preservation set, and γ, they are computed once and reused across task objectives, hyperparameters, and delta parameterizations.

sections.title: 6 CONCLUSION
sections.content: We studied how to incorporate preservation-loss constraint into the model delta parameterization while retaining adaptation flexibility. Our answer is CurvDelta, which estimates local preservation curvature at the pre-adaptation model with block-diagonal K-FAC, retains trailing factor eigendirections via factorwise spectral truncation, and applies two-sided projection so the realized delta remains in this fixed low-curvature space throughout optimization. The same geometry is reusable across tasks and objectives, supports both dense (CurvDelta) and low-rank (CurvLoRA) adaptation, and yields local preservation bound governed jointly by retained curvature and delta magnitude. Across mathematical reasoning, code generation, TOFU, and MUSE, our methods improve the acquisitionretention and forgettingretention trade-offs over baselines, with retention close to the retraining reference. 10 Preprint.

sections.title: A RELATED WORKS
sections.content: Preservation-aware task adaptation. Preservation-aware task adaptation addresses the challenge of acquiring capabilities required by new tasks while limiting degradation of unrelated capabilities previously acquired. Existing approaches differ in both the signal used to identify what should be preserved and the stage of adaptation they constrain. Replay-based methods train on stored examples from earlier tasks, while self-synthesized rehearsal generates proxy examples when the original data are unavailable (Rolnick et al., 2019; Huang et al., 2024). Optimization-based methods instead regularize parameters or reconcile competing objectives: EWC penalizes changes to parameters estimated to be important for earlier tasks (Kirkpatrick et al., 2017), whereas PCGrad, CAGrad, and GradDrop can mediate conflicts between task and preservation gradients when both losses are optimized jointly (Yu et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2021; Chen et al., 2020). PEFT methods constrain the update geometry in different ways. O-LoRA separates successive tasks through orthogonal low-rank subspaces (Wang et al., 2023); MiLoRA adapts minor singular components of pretrained weights; and CorDA provides knowledge-preserved decomposition intended to limit degradation of pretrained knowledge (Wang et al., 2025a; Yang et al., 2024). further line of work explicitly constrains LoRA updates using subspaces derived from pretrained weights, task representations, or both (Xiong & Xie, 2026; Liang & Li, 2024; Luo et al., 2026). These constructions use orthogonality to protect selected parameter or representation subspaces during adaptation. Model editing addresses related preservation problem. ROME and MEMIT directly update selected MLP weights, while MEND learns an auxiliary editor that maps fine-tuning gradients to parameter updates (Meng et al., 2022; 2023; Mitchell et al., 2022). AlphaEdit limits collateral changes by projecting editing perturbations into the null space of preserved-knowledge representations (Fang et al., 2025). CrispEdit projects task gradients into low-curvature space estimated with K-FAC (Ikram et al., 2026). CurvDelta derives its delta space from the local curvature of the preservation loss, relating the allowed update directions to their local preservation cost. It incorporates the projection into the delta parameterization, so that the realized delta remains in the prescribed space throughout optimization, independently of the optimizer. This combines preservation-loss-based choice of geometry with an explicit constraint on the applied delta, supporting both dense and low-rank adaptation. Selective unlearning. LLM unlearning seeks to suppress knowledge or behavior associated with designated forget set while preserving utility on unrelated data, providing practical alternative to full retraining (Cao & Yang, 2015). Existing methods control this trade-off by modifying different objects in the update process. GradDiff couples ascent on the forget-set loss with training on retained data, whereas NPO and SimNPO regulate forgetting through bounded, preference-inspired losses (Liu et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2024; Fan et al., 2025). GRU and SAGO instead reshape the instantaneous update direction using first-order forgetretain signals: GRU projects the unlearning gradient away from directions estimated to harm retention, while SAGO treats unlearning as an asymmetric two-task problem and gates the two gradients coordinate-wise according to their sign agreement (Wang et al., 2025b; Xiao et al., 2026a). LoRA-specific methods control the content or dynamics of the low-rank update. FILA and VILA use parameter-level forget-to-retain importance to initialize adapters, whereas ReGLU uses representation geometry both to initialize discriminative low-rank subspace and to regularize the adapter update away from retained representations (Cha et al., 2025; Kim et al., 2025; Xiao et al., 2026b). Null-space-constrained low-rank adaptation also uses benign hidden representations to restrict updates while combining safe-target response learning with suppression of undesired responses (Ju et al., 2026). Stable Forgetting instead applies bounded transformations to LoRA adapters to control their update dynamics (Garg et al., 2025). SOUL is the second-order counterpart, using second-order information to shape each unlearning step (Jia et al., 2024). CurvDelta derives its delta space from preservation-loss curvature, providing local loss bound in terms of the retained curvature and delta magnitude. Both CurvDelta and CurvLoRA can optimize GradDiff, NPO, or SimNPO within this space. 18 Preprint.
